To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
exposure of rats and mice to diesel exhaust resulted in an increase in inflammatory cells and enzymes in the BAL fluid and in fibrosis in lung tissue.
the inhalation of diluted diesel exhaust caused a dose-dependent increase in the number of inflammatory cells in the BALF of rats and mice, and that the increase was greater in mice than in the rats.
long-term inhalation of diluted diesel exhaust at 0.35 mg soot/m(3) did not cause any adverse effects in either rats or mice.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects of inhaled diesel exhaust on the respiratory tract of laboratory animals and with the usefulness of BAL in detecting the early changes in the lung that accompany the development of chronic lung disease.
the health effects of exposure to diesel exhaust and other combustion products.
the effects of inhaled diesel exhaust on the respiratory system of laboratory animals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, for noncarcinogenic effects, the threshold of exposure to inhaled diesel exhaust is in the range of 0.35 mg soot/m(3) and that this threshold is above environmentally relevant levels.
the inhalation of diesel soot at levels above 0.35 mg/m3 is associated with a chronic inflammation in rodents that is accompanied by the development of fibrosis.
the inhalation of the highest concentration of diluted diesel exhaust tested (7 mg soot/m(3)) caused an inflammatory reaction in the lung, which resulted in a chronic inflammatory response.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the inhalation of diluted diesel exhaust, at the concentrations studied, caused no significant adverse effects in either the rat or mouse, although the rat was more sensitive to the effects of soot deposition in the lung.

the inhalation of diesel particulate at the highest levels tested (7.0 mg/m3) caused an inflammatory reaction in rats and mice, which was accompanied by the formation of focal areas of fibrotic tissue in the rat.
, in the absence of a carcinogenic stimulus, there appears to be a threshold of diesel exhaust exposure for adverse effects on the bronchoaveolar region of the lung.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the analysis of BALF can be used as a sensitive indicator of the early development of pulmonary disease and can be used to differentiate it from normal repair processes.

there is a threshold for the nononcogenic health effects reported here, and that the analysis of BALF is a useful adjunct to chronic toxicity studies to quantitate the development of pulmonary inflammation and fibrosis.
, for the health effects reported in our study, there was no adverse effect below 0.35 mg soot/m(3), the most environmentally relevant level of exposure.
